title: DNA methylation-based prediction of differentiation state at cell-type resolution reveals an age-associated epigenetic mesenchymal drift
summary: Quantifying the differentiation state of cells is an important task in regenerative medicine, cellular reprogramming and in elucidating how differentiation hierarchies are altered in aging and disease. For DNA methylation data (DNAm) there is however an accute shortage of methods for quantifying differentiation state. Here we use machine learning to build EpiDiff, a predictor of differentiation that yields a continuous absolute differentiation index (DI) when applied to a DNAm sample. We extensively validate EpiDiff in single-cells, sorted cells and bulk tissue, as well as in in-vitro differentiation, organoid, reprogramming and cellular rejuvenation experiments. In mixed samples, EpiDiff measures the extent of differentiation across all cellular lineages. In sorted cell populations, we find that DI increases with age and, underpinning this increase, we discover that many cell-types undergo a developmental epigenetic drift that is most prominent towards the mesenchymal lineage. When applied to normal-tissues, EpiDiff is predictive of carcinogenic exposure and cancer risk. In summary, EpiDiff is a unique, general and versatile tool that can accurately quantify the global differentiation state of a DNAm sample with broad applicability to many disciplines.

title: CRISCross: Integration of Epigenetic Information for Deep-Learning-Based Prediction of CRISPR-Cas9 Off-Targets Across Cell Types
summary: CRISPR-Cas9 enables precise genome editing but remains limited by off-target effects, raising safety concerns and necessitating accurate prediction. Although epigenetic features influence Cas9 binding and cleavage, their predictive signals are often weak, highlyvariable, and context-dependent, limiting the effectiveness of existing machine learning approaches. Cross-cell-type settings are especially challenging: epigenetic landscapes differ substantially, and models trained on one cell type frequently fail to generalize. Here, we systematically investigate the role of epigenetic context in off-target prediction and demonstrate that its utility depends on modeling interactions with sequence features rather than treating it as an independent signal. Tabular and deep learning experiments demonstrate that epigenetic features provide a consistent but modestly complementary signal, and that late-stage fusion strategies are insufficient to effectively exploit this information. To address this, we introduce CRISCross, a cross-attention-based architecture that captures sequence-epigenetic interactions at the nucleotide level, alongside CRISPRAT, a synthetic pretraining strategy that learns transferable representations from genome-derived sgRNA-off-target pairs without relying on dataset-specific pretraining. CRISCross, incorporating AlphaGenome-derived chromatin accessibility signals, shows better predictive performance than sequence-only baselines across three independent test datasets spanning two cell types, demonstrating improved generalization across guide RNAs, datasets, and cellular contexts. This is particularly relevant for therapeutic applications involving cell types or patient-derived contexts that lack dedicated experimental datasets. In such settings, predicted chromatin accessibility may provide scalable contextual information when direct epigenomic profiling is unavailable or impractical. Together, these results show that accurate CRISPR off-target prediction benefits from interaction-aware integration of epigenetic context alongside generalizable pretraining strategies.

title: Latent-Space Residue-Pair Networks from Molecular Dynamics Distinguish Ligand-Activated and SAVI-Associated STING
summary: Stimulator of interferon genes (STING) provides an informative model system for developing methods to extract and compare residue-pair fluctuation patterns from molecular dynamics (MD) trajectories. We combined a one-dimensional convolutional autoencoder trained on apo STING with temporal mean pooling, Mahalanobis-distance clustering, and residue-pair similarity networks to compare apo, ligand-bound, and SAVI-associated multi-mutant datasets using 25-dimensional latent descriptors. Networks constructed from clusters capturing state-dependent fluctuation patterns showed lid-dominated organization in the ligand-bound dataset and a1b1-enriched, structurally distributed relationships involving residue 281 in the multi-mutant dataset. These findings identify contrasting residue-pair fluctuation signatures in the analyzed trajectories and provide an interpretable framework for generating hypotheses about ligand-associated and mutation-associated dynamic allostery.

title: AI-guided discovery for low-resource peptide engineering using evolutionary scale modeling
summary: Data scarcity is a major bottleneck in artificial intelligence (AI)-guided peptide engineering, where experimental training sets often contain only tens to a few hundred sequences, and it is difficult to judge in advance whether a protein language model (PLM) will effectively guide iterative discovery before committing to wet-lab work. Here we present SCARSE, a machine learning framework that couples ESM2 protein language model embeddings with Gaussian process regression. Benchmarked across 24 diverse peptide and small-protein datasets spanning substitution and indel variants, antimicrobial peptides, and hemolytic peptides, SCARSE significantly outperformed hand-engineered descriptor baselines on substitution and indel tasks in low-data regimes (20-500 training samples) and performed comparably on short non-mutant peptides. In active learning simulations it consistently prioritized high-performing candidates, discovering up to 7-fold more top-tier peptides than random sampling. Cross-validation (CV) R2 correlated strongly with final active learning performance (Pearson r = 0.80-0.84), and evaluating on as few as 50 labeled peptides reduced CV R2 variance enough for it to serve as a practical, data-efficient criterion for assessing model suitability before iterative screening. SCARSE thus provides an early diagnostic indicator for active learning success and is freely available as an open-source Python package (pip) and through an interactive Hugging Face Spaces web interface.

title: TopFor: Automated Preparation of AMBER-Compatible Parameters for Noncanonical Amino Acids in Peptides
summary: Peptides containing noncanonical amino acids (ncAAs) are becoming increasingly important in drug discovery, but their molecular dynamics (MD) simulation remains limited by labor-intensive residue parameterization and topology preparation. Here, we present TopFor (Topology and Residue Force-Field Parameter Preparation), an open-source, peptide-oriented workflow that automates the generation of ncAA residue templates and force-field parameter files for MD simulations with AMBER using established charge-derivation methods. TopFor supports single-residue, whole-peptide, and batch parameterization workflows. The workflow was validated using the MDM2-p53 complex by comparing native AMBER residue definitions with residues processed by TopFor using three charge-derivation methods, each evaluated in three independent 100 ns MD simulations. TopFor-generated residue definitions showed structural and conformational behavior comparable to the native AMBER representation. Applicability to more complex peptide architectures was demonstrated using the head-to-tail cyclic peptide cyclosporin A and the cyclic depsipeptide cyclohexylgriselimycin. At library scale, 1,138 of 1,214 cyclohexylgriselimycin derivatives (93.7%) successfully completed TopFor parameterization and the subsequent initial AMBER-based computational workflow across two derivatization campaigns. TopFor was further integrated into a structure-based peptide discovery workflow based on the DnaN-griselimycin complex. Six GM-derived peptides were computationally prioritized and experimentally evaluated, of which four produced SPR responses against Mycobacterium smegmatis (M. smegmatis) DnaN and three showed concentration-dependent responses. TopFor reduces the manual effort required to prepare ncAA-containing peptides for MD simulations and enables their integration into both library-scale computational screening and structure-based peptide discovery workflows. Keywords: noncanonical amino acids; peptide parameterization; molecular dynamics; AMBER; AmberTools; peptide design; high-throughput virtual screening

title: An Expert-Curated Benchmark for Frontier and Local LLMs Querying a Biomedical Knowledge Graph
summary: We combine GeneNetwork's 1TB structured database with its metadata as an RDF graph and an associated literature corpus. We benchmark frontier and local LLMs querying it through four architectures: document, graph and agentic retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and a combination of the three. We evaluate them on 40 domain specific expert-curated questions with a new metric: the satisfaction frequency psi (psi, i.e, the share of questions answered with precision and recall of at least 70% or an f1 of at least 60%). psi ranks systems the same way precision, recall and f1 -- a machine learning metric built from the harmonic mean of precision and recall -- but is easier to read and assess for humans. System architecture had a large effect: with full use of Claude Opus 4.8 the plain document RAG of our earlier GNQA system had a psi of 36% against 86% for our new combined tools. Delegating most of the work from Claude Opus 4.8 to a local model halved query costs while still reaching a psi of 59%.

title: AmyloCore-ML: AI/Machine Learning Enabled Identification of Amyloid Fibril Core Regions Using Protein Language Models
summary: Identification of amyloid forming regions in proteins remains central to understanding of their aggregation behaviour, which are central to various neurodegenerative and systemic disorders. Many predictors have been designed to identify amyloid forming regions, however they may not necessarily identify total residues found in actual disease associated fibril structures. To address this, we formed a sequence-based based predictor-AmyloCore-ML to ascertain structural amyloid-core propensity. The predictor was developed using experimentally determined fibril structures obtained from Amyloid Atlas. Ordered residues in the experimental structures were designated as core, and unresolved sampled from the same proteins as matched controls as non-core. Core and non-core regions were encoded using various physicochemical descriptors and protein language model (PLM) embeddings (ESM-2, ANKH, ProtT5) and evaluated using protein-grouped cross-validation. PLMs consistently outperformed physicochemical descriptors, with the best models reaching AUROC values of ~0.88 and AUPRC values of ~0.85. Locked full-length protein scans further localized experimental cores, with ESM-2/ExtraTrees achieving AUROC 0.833, AUPRC 0.751, and a mean peak distance of 12.4 residues. In comparative benchmarking, our predictor showed better performance metrics than CrossBeta and AggrescanAI. The framework therefore provides residue-resolved prediction of structurally incorporated amyloid-core regions directly from sequence.

title: Cell Painting and machine learning for mechanistic profiling of hepatotoxic botanicals and their constituents
summary: BACKGROUND Botanicals are widely consumed as herbal remedies and plant-derived products, but their complex and variable chemical composition presents major challenges for safety assessment. Although hepatotoxicity has been reported for several botanicals, the constituent compounds responsible and the underlying mechanisms often remain poorly characterised. OBJECTIVES We aimed to determine whether Cell Painting could identify candidate constituent drivers of botanical bioactivity and generate hypotheses about potential mechanisms of action in primary human hepatocytes. METHODS We profiled 13 botanical extracts and 85 known constituents across multiple concentrations using Cell Painting alongside assays of metabolic activity and membrane integrity. To interpret morphological phenotypes, we trained machine-learning models using a Cell Painting reference atlas of >1,000 chemicals linked to ToxCast/Tox21 molecular and cellular bioactivity annotations. RESULTS Cell Painting detected bioactivity in 11/13 botanical extracts and 46/85 constituents, compared with 9/13 extracts and 40/85 constituents in the cell-health assays, and generally detected activity at lower concentrations. For 9/13 extracts, at least one constituent was active at a lower concentration than the corresponding botanical extract, supporting the contribution of a subset of potent constituents to mixture-level responses. Aristolochia and goldenseal were the most potent extracts across Cell Painting and cell-health assays and contained highly active constituents. Reference-atlas models generated specific mechanistic hypotheses, including cytotoxicity-, endocrine-, and genotoxicity-associated responses for several botanicals and constituents. CONCLUSION These results support Cell Painting combined with machine learning as a sensitive approach for characterising cellular responses to botanicals, prioritising candidate constituent drivers of hepatotoxicity-associated phenotypes, and generating testable hypotheses about potential mechanisms of action.

title: CLEAR-FORCE: A reservoir computing framework for closed-loop brain stimulation
summary: Electrical stimulation of brain activity has emerged as a key therapeutic intervention for neurological diseases. The success of these approaches relies on precisely tuned stimulation parameters. A major challenge is that these parameters should ideally be adjusted in real-time based on changes in brain activity. Closed-loop controllers address this challenge by monitoring brain activity and adapting stimulation according to ongoing changes in neural dynamics. While machine learning has been helpful in this context, closed-loop controllers typically do not adapt in real-time to fluctuations in brain activity. Here, we propose a novel framework based on reservoir computing to train a closed-loop, real-time neural controller. This approach, termed CLEAR-FORCE, trains the output weights of a recurrent network based on a combination of target signals and feedback from brain activity. Two series of simulations were performed, where the controller was successful at (1) inducing neural oscillations in a population of spiking neurons and (2) suppressing pathological oscillations. This framework provides a promising avenue for the implementation of neural controllers in low-powered, real-time, and adaptive hardware that harnesses machine learning for the personalized treatment of brain disorders.

title: Characterisation of Genetically-Derived Patient Clusters Highlights Genetic Heterogeneity of Inflammatory Bowel Disease
summary: Background and aims. Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD) is a complex immune-mediated condition with a strong genetic contribution. The genetics of IBD are highly complex, with inflammation, autoimmunity, and mucosal immunity pathways involved in its pathogenicity. GenePy is a gene-level disease burden metric. The integration of clinical and genetic data and the application of machine learning methods can aid patient stratification for personalised care. Methods. Lists of consensus IBD pathway genes were curated. GenePy scores were computed from whole exome sequencing data. A K-Means algorithm was optimised using clustering quality and stability metrics on the GenePy scores of genes in each IBD pathway, and the results replicated in three independent IBD cohorts (SPARC IBD, MSCCR IBD, and Southampton IBD). Chi-square tests assessed the association between cluster assignment and phenotypic features, and were multiple test corrected via Benjamini-Hochberg FDR. Results. A strong association was replicated for NOD signalling genes driving IBD subtype, Crohns disease behaviour, and IBD surgery across all cohorts, as well as granuloma in Southampton IBD. This was mainly driven by NOD2. Similar genetic clustering patterns were observed across all cohorts, with additional phenotypic enrichment in clusters driven by NLRP1 (surgery in MSCCR IBD), and nominally significant enrichment for disease behaviour linked to BIRC2 (B2 in Southampton IBD and B2B3 in SPARC IBD). Conclusions. This analysis identified a common genetic architecture across NOD signalling genes across IBD cohorts, replicated a signal for NOD2 as a monogenic driver of disease with a strong phenotypic enrichment, and identified other putative genetic drivers of IBD, such as the NLRP1 gene.

title: Intrinsically disordered regions influence protein motif usage in Drosophila Ubx and AbdA Hox proteins
summary: Hox proteins are evolutionary conserved transcription factors guiding morphogenesis in all bilaterian animals. Conservation mainly concerns the homeodomain (HD), a helix-turn-helix DNA binding motif and flanking sequences close by. Besides, sequences are poorly conserved and disordered. Here we investigate how poorly conserved Intrinsically Disordered Regions (IDRs) influence Hox protein activity, focusing on a closely related Drosophila Hox pair and using a wide range of in vivo function. Studying Drosophila Ultrabithorax (Ubx) and AbdominalA (AbdA) proteins, we find that conserved protein motifs close to the HD are differently used in Ubx and AbdA. Coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations identify a large set of intra-molecular interactions, notably involving poorly conserved disordered regions upstream and downstream the HD. Swapping these regions in Ubx and AbdA alters protein functions and switches motif dependency in some biological situations. This suggests that IDRs, predicted to mediate large and dynamic sets of intramolecular interactions, influence protein motif usage in a context dependent manner.

title: High-throughput variant libraries and machine learning enable robust target-site selection for toehold-switch design in Detectrons
summary: Programmable RNA sensors enable sequence-specific detection of RNA inputs for diagnostics, genetic circuit control, and multiplexed molecular readouts. Although readily programmable, their performance varies substantially with the target site selected within a transcript, making target-site selection a major challenge. Here, we report DeSTAR (Detectron Sensor TARget-site ranker), a machine-learning-assisted target-site ranking model for programmable RNA sensors. To train this model, we generated transcript-wide, single-nucleotide-resolution tiling sensor libraries across six diverse RNA targets, enabling generalization to be tested across transcripts rather than within a single RNA. In leave-one-transcript-out evaluation, DeSTAR's top-ranked sites were enriched for high-performing sensors in held-out transcripts, driven predominantly by interpretable sequence grammar in the sensor stem rather than transcript-specific patterns. Prospectively, on an unseen SARS-CoV-2 transcript, the model's top-ranked sites yielded working sensors roughly five-fold more often than random selection. These results support DeSTAR as a generalizable strategy for target-site selection in RNA sensors across transcripts.

title: Activation of Disease-Associated Polycystin-1 Mutants by Binding of Stalk-derived Agonist Peptides
summary: Polycystin-1 (PC1) functions as an atypical G-protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) with an autocatalytic GAIN domain that cleaves PC1 into extracellular N-terminal (NTF) and membrane-embedded C-terminal (CTF) fragments. Mutations in PC1 are responsible for 85% of autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) cases. Activation of signaling by PC1 CTF has been shown to be allosterically mediated by a stalk tethered agonist (TA) and to be prevented by mutations of the stalk. Soluble, synthetic peptides derived from the PC1 stalk were also shown to re-activate signaling by a stalkless CTF mutant. Here, we have investigated the ability of selected stalk peptide agonists p9, p15 or p17 to re-activate signaling by PC1 CTF with ADPKD-associated missense mutations, G3052R or R3063C. Biochemical experimental data showed that each of the three stalk peptides was able to significantly reactivate signaling by the CTF-R3063C mutant. In contrast, signaling by CTF-G3052R could only be rescued by treatment with p17. In parallel, we employed peptide docking and novel Peptide Gaussian-accelerated Molecular Dynamics (Pep-GaMD) simulations to elucidate the binding conformations of p9, p15 and p17 to the PC1 mutants. The simulation findings were highly consistent with experimental data. Furthermore, Pep-GaMD revealed binding conformations of the agonist peptides and important low-energy conformational states of the PC1 CTF, as well as their critical residue interactions. Overall, our complementary approach provides important mechanistic insights into the re-activation of PC1 disease-associated mutants by stalk-derived peptide agonists. Such insights are expected to be valuable for the future design and development of peptide modulators targeting PC1 for an effective ADPKD therapeutic treatment.

title: Structural Basis for the Rational Design of UAMC-1110-Based FAP Radiopharmaceuticals
summary: Radioligands targeting fibroblast activation protein alpha (FAP) are promising tools for cancer diagnosis and therapy. However, the molecular binding mode of clinically established UAMC-1110-derived ligands such as FAPI-46 remains insufficiently characterized. To simplify synthesis while preserving key binding properties, we designed two novel derivatives - FAP-DD-101 (short aminoalkyl linker) and FAP-DD-102 (extended aminohexanoic acid spacer) - and evaluated them alongside FAPI-46 using molecular docking and all-atom molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. Across all derivatives, we identified a highly stable, energetically favorable charge-anchored binding mode, in which the 2-cyano-4,4-difluoropyrrolidine head anchors in a negatively charged subregion formed by Glu202, Glu203, and Glu204, mimicking the binding architecture observed in the FAP-linagliptin complex. MD trajectories confirmed that FAPI-46 and FAP-DD-101 maintain exceptional stability in this pose, with several non-anchored FAPI-46 trajectories spontaneously evolving toward engagement with this electrostatic subregion. For FAP-DD-102, linker elongation slightly reduced pose robustness, yet initial charge-anchored states still yielded superior average binding energies and vector stability compared to non-anchored poses. Overall, these findings elucidate the key structural determinants of FAP recognition, establishing a rational framework for designing synthetically accessible FAPI radiotracers with retained binding stability.

title: Positive selection and structural disruption of KCNA5 by mutation in colorectal cancer
summary: Ion channels regulate cell proliferation, survival and migration, but the functional consequences of many ion channel mutations in cancer are unknown, and electrophysiological characterisation at scale is impractical. Here we use the mutational landscape of colorectal adenocarcinoma as a functional filter to identify potassium channel mutations under selection. A dN/dS screen of 16 potassium channels expressed in the large intestine identified KCNA5 (Kv1.5) as the strongest candidate under positive mutational selection. These mutations cluster in the T1 tetramerisation, S1-S4 voltage-sensor and pore domains, yet avoid the selectivity filter, indicating that selection does not favour loss of conduction. Within the pore region, the observed mutations occupy a biophysical space distinct from known C-type inactivation, activation-gate and toxin-binding mutations. In the voltage sensor, mutations affect gating-charge arginines. In the T1 domain, mutations fall on inter-subunit interfaces conserved across the KCNA family, and saturation mutagenesis energy calculations predict that they destabilise subunit contacts or the folding of the domain. Molecular dynamics simulations of D166N and G128R show loss of coordinated interface dynamics and distortion of the local backbone, respectively. Transcriptomic analysis of KCNA5-mutant tumours shows reduced expression of cell-cycle, KRAS-related and inflammatory pathways, and we observe differences between transcriptional effects induced by T1 and S1-S4 domain mutations. These changes are not reproduced by low KCNA5 expression alone, consistent with an effect specific to the mutant protein. Together, these computational results highlight that KCNA5 is under mutational selection in colorectal adenocarcinoma, and that these mutations are likely functional and induce phenotypic effects on tumors.

title: Structure-Based Drug Design of Novel Inhibitors Targeting the Thiamine Biosynthesis Pathway in Bacteria
summary: Current generation antibiotics are limited by poor target selectivity and are often mismanaged, leading to widespread antimicrobial resistance. The bacterial thiamine biosynthesis pathway offers compelling alternative since it is highly essential for bacterial survival and yet absent in humans. Genetic perturbations within pathway lead to documented auxotrophy and virulence defects, indicating low mutational tolerance within this pathway. Thiamine phosphate synthase is a key bottleneck enzyme performing the crucial role of coupling thiazole and pyrimidine moieties to form thiamine monophosphate. To develop a suitable inhibitor against it, a structure-based drug design pipeline was implemented. High-throughput virtual screening of nearly 1.5 million molecules provided sufficient exploration of chemical space. Further, R-group substitution was utilized for lead optimization. Structure-Activity Relationship analysis upon molecular mutants reveals patterns among R-group interactions to catalytic residues across various scaffolds. Additionally, ADMET screening and validation using molecular dynamics simulations resulted in a potent orally bioavailable broad-spectrum bactericidal molecule.

title: Human Metalloenzymes Are Disproportionately Linked to Disease: The HEAM Structural Annotation Resource
summary: Catalytic metal-binding sites are established drug targets for many human diseases, yet systematic study of how metal function relates to disease is limited by the lack of a resource combining structural localization of human metal-binding sites with catalytic annotation at scale. We introduce HEAM (the Human Enzymatic Annotation of Metalloproteins), a structurally annotated dataset of 1,933 human metalloenzymes and 1,171 non-catalytic metalloproteins. HEAM incorporates annotated metals into protein structures at their corresponding binding sites and classifies each site as catalytic or non-catalytic using the machine learning classifier MAHOMES II. HEAM more than quadruples the human site-level coverage of the largest prior metalloenzyme database. Using HEAM, we show that human metalloproteins are significantly enriched in KEGG disease pathways relative to the human proteome, and that metalloenzymes specifically are significantly enriched in ClinVar pathogenic variants -- a distinction obscured in prior, catalytically unresolved metalloprotein datasets. These pathogenic variants are concentrated in metabolic disorders, indicating that metabolic dysfunction is a substantial contributor to metalloenzyme-linked disease. By pairing 3D structural annotation with catalytic classification, HEAM provides both a foundation for structure-guided drug design against metal-binding sites and a resource for determining how catalytic and non-catalytic metal function contribute to human disease.
